title: Lost in Translation, Found in Embeddings: Sign Language Translation and Alignment
claim: One model handles two distinct tasks on the same input, with the task selected purely by a text prompt.
layout: Single stacked column, bottom-to-top flow, two color-coded prompt columns under one model bar
description: A vertical bottom-to-top diagram. At the bottom is a filmstrip of ten video frames of a man in a blue shirt signing against changing street backgrounds. Beneath it is a frame-index axis running 0 to 500. Above the filmstrip are two prompt boxes. The left, light blue, holds the translation prompt: 'Using only the sign language, generate a natural and grammatically correct sentence.' The right, light green, holds the alignment prompt, which asks the model to predict start and end frame indices for a given input sentence. Grey arrows lead from each prompt up to a wide pink 'Unified Model' bar. Two more arrows lead to the outputs at the top. The left output is the spoken-language sentence 'But in fact he has an extraordinary super power'. The right output is the frame range '101-239'. The eye goes first to the pink bar and the bold output text.
caption: A unified sign language understanding model. Given signing data, our model performs both SLT and SSA, guided by textual prompts. For both tasks, a 500-frame (20s at 25 fps) video is used as input. In SLT mode, the model receives the sign video with frame-level timestamps specifying the region of interest (not shown for clarity), and generates a spoken language translation for that segment. In SSA mode, the model takes the sign video, a target sentence along with its audio-aligned timestamps (if available), and predicts the timestamps where the sentence is signed.
abstract: Our aim is to develop a unified model for sign language understanding, that performs sign language translation (SLT) and sign-subtitle alignment (SSA). Together, these two tasks enable the conversion of continuous signing videos into spoken language text and also the temporal alignment of signing with subtitles -- both essential for practical communication, large-scale corpus construction, and educational applications. To achieve this, our approach is built upon three components: (i) a lightweight visual backbone that captures manual and non-manual cues from human keypoints and lip-region images while preserving signer privacy; (ii) a Sliding Perceiver mapping network that aggregates consecutive visual features into word-level embeddings to bridge the vision-text gap; and (iii) a multi-task scalable training strategy that jointly optimises SLT and SSA, reinforcing both linguistic and temporal alignment. To promote cross-linguistic generalisation, we pretrain our model on large-scale sign-text corpora covering British Sign Language (BSL) and American Sign Language (ASL) from the BOBSL and YouTube-SL-25 datasets. With this multilingual pretraining and strong model design, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the challenging BOBSL (BSL) dataset for both SLT and SSA. Our model also demonstrates robust zero-shot generalisation and finetuned SLT performance on How2Sign (ASL), highlighting the potential of scalable translation across different sign languages.
